html:
The Black Death reached Constantinople in 1347, making it one of the first cities of Europe to be struck. The plague came by sea from the Black Sea ports, where it had broken out among the Golden Horde besieging the Genoese town of Caffa in Crimea, and ships carried it on through the Bosporus to the Mediterranean.

Among the dead was Andronikos, the young son of Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, who had just won the civil war. The emperor later described the disease in his history, modelled on Thucydides' account of the plague of Athens: swellings in the groin and armpits, spitting of blood, and death within days. A large share of the city died, though there are no reliable numbers.

The plague came on top of war and poverty, and it returned again and again over the next century, just as the Ottomans were crossing into Europe. The capital that had once held hundreds of thousands was by 1453 a city of perhaps fifty thousand.
